The Story of Yam Muni

I bow to the gods, the guru, and the word of Lord Jina, and I write the story of the monk Yam, who despite having very little knowledge, made himself worthy of liberation and ultimately attained moksha. This story bestows happiness upon all who hear it.

In the land of Udra stood a famous and beautiful city named Dharm. Its king was Yam — wise and learned in the scriptures. His queen was Dhanvati, who bore a son named Gardabh and a daughter named Konika. Konika was exceedingly beautiful. Besides Dhanvati, the king had several other queens, and in total he had five hundred sons. All five hundred brothers were virtuous and detached from worldly life. The royal minister was named Deergh, a man of great intelligence and skill in statecraft. With all these blessings, the king was very happy and governed his kingdom in peace.

One day a royal astrologer examined Konika's features and told the king, "Maharaj, the princess is most fortunate. Whoever becomes her husband shall be master of the entire earth." The king was overjoyed and from that day guarded her with great care. He had a magnificent underground chamber built for her, so that no powerful king of lesser rank might set eyes on her.

One day a group of five hundred monks arrived in his capital, led by the great ascetic Sudharmacharya, whose sole vow was the welfare of the world. With great joy and enthusiasm, all the citizens went forth to worship the Acharya, carrying various offerings in their hands. Seeing them go, the king too set out — but swollen with pride in his own learning, he went speaking ill of the monks. By reviling the saints and being arrogant about his knowledge, such a powerful karmic obstruction arose that all his intelligence was destroyed at once. He became utterly foolish.

Therefore, those who are noble and wish to become truly wise should never be proud of their knowledge — nor of lineage, caste, strength, supernatural powers, wealth, body, austerity, worship, or honour. Pride in any of these brings great suffering.

Seeing his condition, the king regained his composure. Like a tuskless elephant, he became free of pride. He deeply repented for his actions and bowed to the great monk with devotion. Sudharmacharya, seeing his sincere repentance, taught him the path of dharma. The king accepted the twelve vows of a layman and spent his remaining days in pious service and meditation.

Though Yam had acquired only limited scriptural knowledge, his sincere repentance and devotion transformed him. He renounced worldly life, became a monk, and through dedicated practice, destroyed his karmas and attained liberation.

This story teaches that pride — especially pride in knowledge — is a great obstacle on the spiritual path. Even a learned king can be reduced to foolishness by arrogance. But sincere repentance and humble devotion can redeem anyone, no matter how far they have fallen. The door to liberation is open to all who approach it with humility.
